passages.title: Questions 1–5
passages.body:
Not all agricultural societies become civilizations, but no civilization can become one without passing through the stage of agriculture. This is because at some stage in the development of agriculture, as productivity improves, not all people would need to be engaged in producing or procuring food. A significant number of people could be freed up to pursue other activities such as building walls or monuments for new cities; making new tools, weapons and jewellery; organizing long-distance trade; creating new artistic masterpieces; coming up with new inventions; keeping accounts; and perhaps constructing new public infrastructure such as irrigation canals that further improve the productivity of agriculture, thus realizing even more people to do new things.

This can happen, of course, only if a society that has transitioned to high-productivity agriculture has also, at some stage in its evolution, found a way to channel the bonanza of free time into other work fruitfully. In the ancient world, this often involved creating new ideologies and new hierarchies or power structures to coerce or otherwise convince large groups of people to devote their time to the new tasks for very little reward.
passages.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

passages.title: Questions 6–10
passages.body:
When we pick up a newspaper, a book, or an article, we come to our task with certain preconceptions and predispositions. We expect to find a specific piece of information or be presented with an argument or an analysis of something, say, the likelihood of recession in the next six months or the reasons why children can't read. We probably know a little about the book or article we are reading even before we start. There was, after all, some reason why we chose to read one piece of writing rather than another.

Our expectations and predispositions may, however, blind us to what the article and its author is actually saying. If, for example, we are used to disagreeing with the author, we may see only what we expect to see and not what is actually there. Day after day in our routine pattern of life we expose ourselves to the same newspaper, the same magazine, even books by authors with the same perspectives. In order to reflect on our reading habits and improve our skills we need to break out of this routine, step back and look at what we are doing when we read.

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.theme: Agriculture and the rise of civilizations
questions.question: Which one of the following statements is true according to the author?
questions.opt_a: Agriculture has always been part of all civilizations.
questions.opt_b: Not all civilizations have undergone the processes of agriculture.
questions.opt_c: Agriculture gave birth to new civilizations.
questions.opt_d: Communities discontinued agriculture to become civilizations.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Use only what the passage says.
Step 1: The author says 'no civilization can become one without passing through the stage of agriculture', so agriculture is part of every civilization's history.
Step 2: (b) and (d) contradict this. (c) is wrong because the author says not all agricultural societies become civilizations.
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.theme: Surplus food frees people for other work
questions.question: A significant number of people were sent to carry out other work from agriculture because
questions.opt_b: people were needed to build monuments, weapons, jewellery, etc.
questions.opt_d: this enabled the development of civilizations.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Cause and effect in a passage.
Step 1: As productivity improves, not all people are needed to produce food, so many are freed for other work.
Step 2: That means there was enough (sufficient) farm produce.
Answer: (c).

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.question: What kind of agriculture based societies would emerge as civilizations?
questions.opt_a: Societies which achieved high productivity in agriculture had the opportunity to find time for other work.
questions.opt_b: Societies which depended on agriculture completely moved to other fruitful work so as to move to many places.
questions.opt_c: Societies which transitioned from one stage of agriculture to another.
questions.opt_d: Societies which could not do agriculture for lack of resources moved to other work.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Match the option to the author's condition.
Step 1: The author says it happens 'only if a society that has transitioned to high-productivity agriculture' finds a way to use the free time fruitfully.
Step 2: Only (a) states this.
Answer: (a).

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.question: Which word in the passage means 'changeover'?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Vocabulary in context.
Step 1: A changeover is a move from one state to another. 'Transitioned' means moved or changed from one stage to another.
Step 2: 'Channel' means direct, 'coerce' means force, 'hierarchies' means ranked orders.
Answer: (a).

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.theme: What the author does not say about readers
questions.question: According to the author, which one of the following statements is not true?
questions.opt_b: Readers have expectations when they read an article or a book.
questions.opt_c: Readers look for specific information in any of their readings.
questions.opt_d: Readers assume that everything they read will have new information.
questions.explanation:
Concept: A 'not true' item needs the one statement the passage does not support.
Step 1: (a), (b), (c) match the passage: preconceptions and expectations shape reading, and readers expect a 'specific piece of information'.
Step 2: The passage never says readers assume everything will be new.
Answer: (d).

Answer: (a).

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.theme: Verb form after a time reference
questions.question:
Directions: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose (d).

__After mysteriously expanding for decades,__ (a) __Antarctica's sea ice cover__ (b) __starting melting.__ (c)
questions.explanation:
Concept: The action is complete, so the past tense is needed.
Step 1: 'After expanding for decades, the ice cover started melting' needs 'started', not 'starting'.
Answer: (c).

questions.explanation:
Concept: An auction is not itself 'price based'; the price is decided by a method.
Step 1: Part (b) should read 'will be priced', so that the sentence says the price will be set using the multiple price method.
Step 2: UPSC's official key marks (b).
Answer: (b).

questions.subject: Sentence Organisation
questions.topic: Ordering of Sentences in a Passage
questions.question:
Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: Chinua Achebe was born in 1930 and educated at the Government College in Umuahia, Nigeria.
S6: Chinua Achebe has written over twenty books, including novels, stories, essays and collections of poetry, and won the Nobel Prize for literature.
P: During the Civil War in Nigeria, he worked for the Biafran government service.
Q: After the War, he was appointed Senior Research Fellow at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka.
R: He joined the Nigerian Broadcasting Company in Lagos in 1954, later becoming its Director of External Broadcasting.
S: He received a BA from London University in 1953 and in 1956 he studied broadcasting in London at the BBC.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the opening idea, then follow the links (this, then, however).
Step 1: The life story runs in time order: BA in 1953 and BBC study (S), joined the broadcaster (R), the Civil War (P), then after the War (Q).
Answer: (a) SRPQ.
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Sentence Organisation
questions.topic: Ordering of Sentences in a Passage
questions.question:
Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: “Every person carries in his head a mental model of the world — a subjective representation of external reality,” writes Alvin Toffler in Future Shock.
S6: When we begin to think we can do so only because our mind is already filled with all sorts of ideas with which to think.
P: It organizes our knowledge and gives us a place from which to argue.
Q: This mental model is, he says, like a giant filing cabinet.
R: It contains a slot for every item of information coming to us.
S: As E.F. Schumacher says, “When we think, we do not just think; we think ideas.”
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the opening idea, then follow the links (this, then, however).
Step 1: Q introduces the filing cabinet image, R says what it contains, P says what it does, and S (Schumacher) leads into S6 about ideas.
Answer: (c) QRPS.

questions.subject: Sentence Organisation
questions.topic: Ordering of Sentences in a Passage
questions.question:
Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: People in society need many goods and services in their everyday life including food, clothing, shelter, transport, etc.
S6: The teacher in the local school has the skills required to impart education to the students.
P: A weaver may have some yarn, some cotton and other instruments required for weaving cloth.
Q: A family farm may own a plot of land, some grains, farming implements, maybe a pair of bullocks and also the labour services of the family members.
R: Every individual has some amount of the goods and services that one would like to use.
S: In fact, the list of goods and services that any individual needs is so large that no individual in society, to begin with, has all the things one needs.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the opening idea, then follow the links (this, then, however).
Step 1: S1 says people need many goods and services. 'In fact' (S) adds that nobody has all of them. R says each person has some. Then the examples run Q (family farm), P (weaver) and S6 (teacher).
Answer: (d) SRQP.
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Sentence Organisation
questions.topic: Ordering of Sentences in a Passage
questions.question:
Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: Farming is the main production activity in the village.
S6: The new ways of farming need less land, but much more capital.
P: These have allowed the farmers to produce more crops from the same amount of land.
Q: Over the years there have been many important changes in the way farming is practised.
R: But in raising production, a great deal of pressure has been put on land and other natural resources.
S: This is an important achievement, since land is fixed and scarce.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the opening idea, then follow the links (this, then, however).
Step 1: Changes in farming (Q), these allowed more crops (P), an important achievement (S), but pressure on resources (R), leading to the new ways of S6.
Answer: (a) QPSR.
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Sentence Organisation
questions.topic: Ordering of Sentences in a Passage
questions.question:
Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: Britain was the first country to experience modern industrialization.
S6: This gave people a wider choice for ways to spend their earnings and expanded the market for the sale of goods.
P: This meant that the kingdom had common laws, a single currency and a market that was not fragmented by local authorities and uneven taxation.
Q: It had been politically stable since the seventeenth century, with England, Wales and Scotland unified under a monarchy.
R: By then a large section of the people received their income in the form of wages and salaries than in goods.
S: By the end of the seventeenth century, money was widely used as the medium of exchange.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the opening idea, then follow the links (this, then, however).
Step 1: Political stability (Q), so common laws and currency (P), money widely used by the end of the century (S), 'By then' wages replaced goods (R), leading to S6.
Answer: (a) QPSR.
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Sentence Organisation
questions.topic: Ordering of Sentences in a Passage
questions.question:
Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: For several million years, humans lived by hunting wild animals and gathering wild plants.
S6: As a result, conditions were favourable for the growth of grasses such as wild barley and wheat.
P: This led to the development of farming and pastoralism as a way of life.
Q: This change took place because the last ice age came to an end about 13,000 years ago and with that warmer, wetter conditions prevailed.
R: Then, between 10,000 and 4,500 years ago, people in different parts of the world learnt to domesticate certain plants and animals.
S: The shift from foraging to farming was a major turning point in the human history.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the opening idea, then follow the links (this, then, however).
Step 1: People domesticated plants and animals (R), which led to farming (P), a major turning point (S), caused by the end of the ice age (Q). 'As a result' in S6 then follows Q.
Answer: (d) RPSQ.
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Sentence Organisation
questions.topic: Ordering of Sentences in a Passage
questions.question:
Directions: S1 and S6 are fixed. Arrange P, Q, R and S in between so that the six sentences form a coherent passage.

S1: All governments claim eternal consistency and success.
S6: Diplomacy offers choices, and those choices must be negotiated with other sovereign actors.
P: Choices involved uncertainty, risk and immediacy; those who must take the choices operate in the contemporary political milieu.
Q: And yet the essence of governance is choice.
R: Nowhere is this more true than in foreign policy decision-making.
S: Some even claim omniscience.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the opening idea, then follow the links (this, then, however).
Step 1: Governments claim success and even omniscience (S), 'And yet' governance is choice (Q), choices involve risk (P), nowhere more than in foreign policy (R), then diplomacy (S6).
Answer: (a) SQPR.
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.question:

S1: Buddhism continued to spread into many lands of Asia during the period of 5th and 6th century.
S6: He translated several scriptural commentaries into Pali and wrote a work called the Visuddhimagga, which soon attained the status of a classic work on Theravada doctrine and meditation.
P: While this can be understood as a part of larger processes of cultural interaction, especially trade, a key role was played by monks.
Q: We know a little bit about some of them, but there must have been countless men whose commitment to the Buddhist path gave them the courage and determination to persevere in the face of the long, hard journey to India and back.
R: Buddhism had made its way to Sri Lanka many centuries earlier, during the time of Ashoka, and a thriving Buddhist community soon took root.
S: In the 5th century, the monk Buddhaghosha travelled to Sri Lanka.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Find the opening idea, then follow the links (this, then, however).
Step 1: The spread (S1) was helped by monks (P), many unnamed (Q), Buddhism had reached Sri Lanka earlier (R), and in the 5th century Buddhaghosha went there (S). 'He' in S6 refers to him.
Answer: (c) PQRS.

questions.opt_c: You can meet the officer when he returns from China on Monday.
questions.opt_d: The officer will meet you when you return from China on Monday.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Time clause with 'when'.
Step 1: After 'when' in a future time clause, use the simple present: 'when he returns'.
Answer: (c).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct sentence that combines the given sentences.

He is hard-working. He is honest too.
questions.opt_a: He is not only hard-working, but also honest.
questions.opt_b: He is only hard-working and honest.
questions.opt_c: He is hard-working but honest too.
questions.opt_d: He is not hard-working but also honest.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Not only ... but also.
Step 1: 'Not only ... but also' joins the two qualities and keeps the meaning of 'too'.
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct sentence that combines the given sentences.

Parents have been waiting since morning. They want to meet the counsellor.
questions.opt_a: The counsellor has been waiting to meet the parents since morning.
questions.opt_b: Parents had been waiting to meet the counsellor since the morning.
questions.opt_c: Parents are waiting to meet the counsellor in the morning.
questions.opt_d: Parents have been waiting since morning to meet the counsellor.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Combining with an infinitive.
Step 1: Keep the present perfect continuous and the subject 'Parents', and join the purpose with 'to meet'.
Answer: (d).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct sentence that combines the given sentences.

Which is the correct combination of the given two simple sentences using 'If' clause?

Minchi should have worked hard. She would have cleared the test.
questions.opt_a: If Minchi had worked hard, she would have cleared the test.
questions.opt_b: Had not Minchi worked hard, she could not have cleared the test.
questions.opt_c: If Minchi has worked hard, she would have cleared the test.
questions.opt_d: If Minchi had worked hard, she will have cleared the test.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Third conditional.
Step 1: Third conditional = If + past perfect, would have + past participle.
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct sentence that combines the given sentences.

Which one of the following is the correct statement combining the two statements using 'though'?

He has been trying his level best to win. He could not succeed.
questions.opt_a: Though he is trying his level best to win, he could not succeed.
questions.opt_b: He is trying his level best to win, though he could not succeed.
questions.opt_c: Though he has been trying his level best to win, he could not succeed.
questions.opt_d: Though he had been trying his level best to win, he could not succeed.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Concession with 'though'.
Step 1: Join with 'though' and keep both verbs as given: 'has been trying' and 'could not succeed'. (a) and (b) change the first verb, and (d) shifts it to the past perfect. UPSC's official key marks (c).
Answer: (c).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct sentence that combines the given sentences.

Which is the correct combination of the given two sentences using 'relative clause'?

Gandhiji preached peace. He is an apostle of peace.
questions.opt_a: Gandhiji who preached peace is an apostle of peace.
questions.opt_b: Gandhiji preached peace because he is an apostle of peace.
questions.opt_c: Gandhiji who preached peace is called an apostle of peace.
questions.opt_d: Gandhiji is an apostle of peace because he preached peace.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Relative clause.
Step 1: A relative clause uses 'who'. Only (a) does this without adding new meaning.
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.theme: Past perfect for the earlier action
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct sentence that combines the given sentences.

Priya reached the station. The bus left before her.
questions.opt_a: When Priya reached the station, the bus had already left.
questions.opt_b: When Priya had reached the station, the bus already left.
questions.opt_c: Priya reached the station, when the bus already left.
questions.opt_d: When Priya had reached the station, the bus had already left.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Past perfect for the earlier action.
Step 1: The bus left first, so it takes the past perfect; Priya's arrival is the simple past.
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct sentence that combines the given sentences.

He is too tired. He could not stand.
questions.opt_a: He is so tired that he could scarcely stand.
questions.opt_b: He is too tired and cannot stand.
questions.opt_c: He will not stand and he is very tired.
questions.opt_d: He is so tired that he could not be standing.
questions.explanation:
Concept: So ... that.
Step 1: 'Too ... to' becomes 'so ... that he could scarcely / could not stand'. (b) changes the tense, (c) changes the meaning, and (d) 'could not be standing' is not idiomatic. UPSC's official key marks (a).
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct sentence that combines the given sentences.

The teacher entered the classroom. All students stopped talking.
questions.opt_a: No sooner did the teacher enter the classroom than the students stopped talking.
questions.opt_b: As soon as the teacher entered the classroom all students were asked to stop talking.
questions.opt_c: All students stopped talking as the teacher enters the classroom.
questions.opt_d: No sooner did the students stop talking than the teacher entered the classroom.
questions.explanation:
Concept: No sooner ... than.
Step 1: The teacher entered first, then the students stopped. 'No sooner did + subject + verb ... than' keeps this order.
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct sentence that combines the given sentences.

Which one of the following is the correct statement of the combination of the two sentences given below using 'whereas'?

Kavya is interested in reading books. Her sister shows interest in outdoor games.
questions.opt_a: Kavya is interested in reading books whereas her sister's interest is outdoor games.
questions.opt_b: Kavya is interested in reading books whereas her sister is not interested in it.
questions.opt_c: Kavya is interested in reading whereas her sister's interest is outdoor games.
questions.opt_d: Kavya is interested in reading books whereas her sister's interest is to play outside.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Contrast with 'whereas'.
Step 1: 'Whereas' contrasts the two interests. (a) keeps both facts without adding anything new.
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.topic: Active and Passive Voice / Direct and Indirect Speech
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the given direct speech sentence.

Rahul said to his teacher, “Madam, what is the way to solve the question?”
questions.opt_a: Rahul asked his teacher what the way to solve the question was.
questions.opt_b: Rahul told his teacher what was the way to solve the question.
questions.opt_c: Rahul asked to his teacher what the way was to solve the question.
questions.opt_d: Rahul told his teacher what the way was to solve the question.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reported question.
Step 1: A question is reported with 'asked' and statement word order ('what the way ... was').
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.topic: Active and Passive Voice / Direct and Indirect Speech
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the given direct speech sentence.

He said to his friend, “Could you please close the door?”
questions.opt_a: He requested his friend to close the door.
questions.opt_b: He requested his friend to please close the door.
questions.opt_c: He ordered his friend to close the door.
questions.opt_d: He wanted his friend to close the door for him.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reported request.
Step 1: A polite request with 'please' becomes 'requested ... to ...' and 'please' is dropped.
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.topic: Active and Passive Voice / Direct and Indirect Speech
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the given direct speech sentence.

Raj said to Sheela, “The Sun rises in the east.”
questions.opt_a: Raj told Sheela that the Sun rose in the east.
questions.opt_b: Raj told Sheela that the Sun rises in the east.
questions.opt_c: Raj asked Sheela that the Sun rises in the east.
questions.opt_d: Raj said to Sheela that the Sun has arisen in the east.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Universal truth.
Step 1: A universal truth keeps the present tense when reported.
Answer: (b).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.topic: Active and Passive Voice / Direct and Indirect Speech
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the given direct speech sentence.

Navanitha said to her friends, “What a scintillating beauty it is!”
questions.opt_a: Navanitha told to her friends that it was a scintillating beauty.
questions.opt_b: Navanitha exclaimed to her friends what a scintillating beauty it was.
questions.opt_c: Navanitha asked her friends whether it was a scintillating beauty.
questions.opt_d: Navanitha exclaimed to her friends that it was a scintillating beauty.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reported exclamation.
Step 1: An exclamation is reported with 'exclaimed that' and becomes a statement: 'What a scintillating beauty it is!' becomes 'that it was a scintillating beauty'. UPSC's official key marks (d).
Answer: (d).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.topic: Active and Passive Voice / Direct and Indirect Speech
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the given direct speech sentence.

The Captain said to the soldiers, “March forward and aim at the peak of the hill today.”
questions.opt_a: The Captain requested the soldiers to march forward and aim at the peak of the hill that day.
questions.opt_b: The Captain ordered the soldiers to march forward and aim at the peak of the hill today.
questions.opt_c: The Captain ordered the soldiers to march forward and aim at the peak of the hill that day.
questions.opt_d: The Captain told the soldiers that they should march forward and aim at the peak of the hill that day.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reported command.
Step 1: A command is reported with 'ordered ... to', and 'today' becomes 'that day'.
Answer: (c).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.topic: Active and Passive Voice / Direct and Indirect Speech
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the given direct speech sentence.

“Where were you last evening?” said the lady to her maid.
questions.opt_a: The lady asked her maid where she had been the previous evening.
questions.opt_b: The lady asked her maid where she had been in the last evening.
questions.opt_c: The lady asked her maid where had she been the evening before.
questions.opt_d: The lady told her maid where she had been to the last evening.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reported question with time change.
Step 1: 'Were' becomes 'had been', 'last evening' becomes 'the previous evening', and the word order is that of a statement.
Answer: (a).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.topic: Active and Passive Voice / Direct and Indirect Speech
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the given direct speech sentence.

“Those who sowed the seeds last season will reap the harvest this season,” said the leader to her followers.
questions.opt_a: The leader said to her followers that those who sowed the seeds the previous season would reap the harvest that season.
questions.opt_b: The leader addressed her followers that those who have sown the seeds the previous season would reap the harvest this season.
questions.opt_c: The leader addressed her followers that those who had sown the seeds the previous season would reap the harvest that season.
questions.opt_d: The leader advised her followers that those who sow the seeds the previous season would reap the harvest this season.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reported statement.
Step 1: Backshift every verb: 'sowed' becomes 'had sown' and 'will' becomes 'would'; 'last season' becomes 'the previous season' and 'this season' becomes 'that season'. Only (c) does all of these. UPSC's official key marks (c).
Answer: (c).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.topic: Active and Passive Voice / Direct and Indirect Speech
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the given direct speech sentence.

He said to his manager, “Could you please pass the bill this week?”
questions.opt_a: He told his manager that bill to be passed.
questions.opt_b: He requested his manager to pass the bill that week.
questions.opt_c: He ordered his manager to pass the bill that week.
questions.opt_d: He requested his manager to pass the bill this week.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reported request.
Step 1: A polite request becomes 'requested ... to ...', and 'this week' becomes 'that week'.
Answer: (b).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage
questions.topic: Active and Passive Voice / Direct and Indirect Speech
questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the given direct speech sentence.

The village chief said to the villagers, “All of us need to adopt new regulations. We will protect our Earth forever.”
questions.opt_a: The village chief ordered the villagers that all of them needed to adopt new regulations and they would protect their Earth forever.
questions.opt_b: The village chief told the villagers that all of them need to adopt new regulations and they will protect their Earth forever.
questions.opt_c: The village chief wanted the villagers needed to adopt new regulations and they would protect their Earth forever.
questions.opt_d: The village chief told the villagers that all of them needed to adopt new regulations and they would protect their Earth forever.
questions.explanation:
Concept: Reported statements joined.
Step 1: Pronouns shift ('us' to 'them', 'we' to 'they', 'our' to 'their') and 'will' becomes 'would'.
Answer: (d).
questions.source: CDS I 2020 English set A (set code PLKI-F-ENG – A)

questions.subject: Grammar and Usage

questions.question:
Directions: Choose the correct indirect speech form of the given direct speech sentence.

The grandfather said to the baby, “May you live long with all good things of life.”
questions.opt_a: The grandfather blessed to the baby with long life and all good things of life.
questions.opt_b: The grandfather asked the baby that she would live long with all good things of life.
questions.opt_c: The grandfather wanted the baby to live long with all good things of life.
questions.opt_d: The grandfather blessed the baby that she would live long with all good things of life.

Concept: Reported blessing.
